$comment: Documentation navigation. Hand-maintained: the wiki has no ordering of its own, so this file is the single source of truth for sidebar structure, short nav labels and search-engine descriptions. `kind: "guide"` resolves to content/docs/<slug>.md, which the wiki sync owns; adding `"source": "authored"` reads content/guides/<slug>.md instead, which is authored in this repository and never touched by the sync. `kind: "page"` is a route implemented in src/app.

pages.title: OPEN//77 documentation
pages.description: How OPEN//77 packages gameplay as resources: the session model, the authoritative server, a hello-world manifest, and the conventions shared by every Lua API.

pages.title: Developer Preview is live
pages.description: Start using the active OPEN//77 Developer Preview: account approval, downloads, hosting, the Lua API, experimental features and reporting bugs.

pages.title: The Workshop: install and share resources
pages.description: The free OPEN//77 Workshop: paste a creation link into Warden to install, update or roll back a resource; publish your own as a ZIP or GitHub release with screenshots and a hover clip; what moderators check, versions, licenses, discussion and the upload rejection reasons.

pages.title: How OPEN//77 works
pages.description: What OPEN//77 is and is not, how players connect, why it is built on dedicated servers rather than peer-to-peer sessions, the project roadmap, and answers to the questions people ask most.

pages.title: The OPEN//77 launcher
pages.description: The player's guide to the OPEN//77 launcher: installing it, the SmartScreen warning on an unsigned executable and what it actually means, signing in, how it verifies your game build, the mod menu and everything it refuses to do silently, joining a world, direct-connect links, how it updates itself, and where its log is.

pages.title: Build resources with an AI agent
pages.description: Install the OPEN//77 Devkit MCP in one line and give Claude Code, Codex, Cursor or VS Code every Lua native, permission, event and game-data name, pinned to the server build you run.

pages.title: Host your own server
pages.description: A step-by-step guide to running your own OPEN//77 dedicated server: get the Windows or Linux build, mint a license key, walk the first-run setup, edit server.jsonc, launch it, and watch it appear automatically in the launcher.

pages.title: Server licensing
pages.description: How a server joins the OPEN//77 platform: create an account, mint a license key in the keymaster, put the key in your server config, and how the master authorises the server on boot.

pages.title: Warden
pages.description: Warden is the OPEN//77 in-server admin panel: a browser control room for live console, Lua resources, players, configuration and admins. Review operations that require a restart.

pages.title: Manage Workshop resources with Warden
pages.description: Install a Workshop creation from its pasted link, review the plan, update, uninstall and roll back; the Workshop chip in the Resources tab, revoked releases, preload restart staging, local configuration and retained backups.
The live roster in Warden — ping, health, life state, match — and the per-row admin actions: warn, kick, ban, grant rights, heal, freeze and move, plus why spectate cannot be adapted from a browser.

pages.title: Your server in the launcher
pages.description: How the OPEN//77 launcher reaches your world: how a server appears in the browser at all, what a catalogue row actually carries, the open77:// deep-link contract for your own Join buttons, what a connecting player must have, and how a world declares the mods every player must load.

pages.title: Branding your server
pages.description: Give your server an icon and a banner from the Warden panel, with no SSH and no restart: what the two images are, the real size and shape limits (including the combined budget that decides whether your server is listed at all), and what to check when an image does not appear.
Exporting a public identity, whitelisting a player, and declaring restricted server commands behind the access control list.
Durable player identifiers, session-scoped ids, display names, the rename flow, and what a game server can actually verify about a connecting player.
Connect events, admission deferrals, whitelists, bans and disconnect reasons.
Resource manifests, the client and server runtime split, signing and download, hot reload, and the security model around resources the server hands to connecting players.

pages.title: The Lua resource runtime
pages.description: What a resource actually gets: the complete manifest reference, the scheduler and lifecycle events, local and network events, modules and cross-resource exports, the core Open77 namespaces, WebUI surfaces, and every sandbox quota.
`vector2`, `vector3`, `vector4`, `vec` and `quat` in both Lua runtimes: arithmetic, swizzles, `#` for magnitude, distance helpers — and the guarantee that plain tables keep working everywhere.

Every dedicated-server global, Open77 namespace, permission, constant and result shape: scheduler, events, commands, players, combat, routing buckets, loot, vehicles, NPCs, elevators, database and logging.
Publish and call asynchronous exports across isolated server resources: complete Lua examples, caller identity, permissions, safe values, timeouts and reload behavior.
Every client export published by the official OPEN//77 resource packages, with signatures per package and how to call them safely across resources.
Local modules, published dependency libraries and `require`: the per-resource cache, the permissions a module runs under, what reload does to it, and how a module differs from an export.

Ask the other side a question and wait for the answer: `Open77.callbacks` in both directions, promise results, per-resource namespacing, timeouts, limits and why a callback is a request rather than a grant.
Key/value state attached to the server, a player or an entity that replicates itself: selectors, change handlers, who is entitled to see what, the caps, and why a client can never write a bag.

pages.title: The join-time readiness gate
pages.description: Open77.ready: the host-owned barrier that stops one resource teleporting, spawning or killing a player another resource is not finished with. Holds, timeouts, the session number, and the rule every gamemode must follow.

pages.title: Operator tunables
pages.description: Open77.tunables: declaring the numbers a server owner may retune live from the admin panel, the file-scope local that silently defeats it, and choosing between live, promote and per-match capture.
Endpoint- and resource-isolated local key/value persistence: CRUD, search, atomic operations, quotas, and why it must never hold secrets.

The `Citizen` table, `SetTick`, generic promises and the shared-script helpers that let a FiveM script run unchanged, the three places OPEN//77 deliberately answers differently, and what is still missing.

Query native player states and apply resource-owned movement, aim and firing restrictions. Includes IsPlayer checks, FreezePosition, FreezeRotation, Allow controls, permissions and replication limits.
Enable synchronized blue holocall eye glow with server-owned Lua leases, automatic cleanup, routing-bucket snapshots and local/F7 presentation.
Read player statistics and control health, stamina and regeneration.
Weapon templates, slots, holstering and server assignments.
Enumerate the other players a client can already see — ids, bodies, distances and the nearest one — with no permission at all, and why a player id does not outlive a body.
Hold a player's body still: the authoritative server freeze on the engine's own movement restriction, the presentation-local client hold, what a freeze stops and what it deliberately does not.
Move the local player's body and know when it has really arrived: the two teleports and why there are two, what “settled” actually tests, raw settle tickets, noclip and the map pick.
Spawn Character records directly; manage streaming, authority, tasks, health and replicated behavior.
Control AI, combat, perception and voice lines per NPC with authoritative server Lua APIs.
Search 6,582 Character records, copy spawn IDs and inspect appearances and compatibility warnings.
Authoritative ground drops: creating and projecting item drops, validating pickups, the onLootPickup hook, and where native UI ends and server authority begins.
Player preferences, server policy and camera ownership.

How synchronized role-play animations work: install the service, build your first Lua action, use the /anim menu, manage sequences and cancellation, and understand client/server authority and temporary third person.
Browse 15 RP profiles and 73 exact clip variants, including giving, examination and wounded poses, with placement, rig bindings and experimental playback coverage.

Coordinate giving, healing, carrying and escorting: server reservations, player consent, shared animation timing, Lua examples and safe cancellation. Requires matching client/server builds and the player-interactions system resource.

`open77_rp_basics`: cuff, escort and search composed from primitives that already shipped, how a hold always ends, and why `carry` refuses instead of faking a player-to-player attachment this engine does not have.
Control photo mode from a client resource, with exclusive ownership and cleanup.
Build multiplayer cyberware with server-owned implants, configurable grades, persistent installation, native presentation and permission-controlled Lua APIs.
Add native Gorilla Arms to your server: normal and charged punches, synchronized knockback, configurable damage and cosmetics, plus Lua installation examples and optional doctor and arena resources.

Native ground and air dash as a server-owned session grant: definitions, charges, stamina and cooldown, one Air Dash per airtime, correlated `onDashChanged` / `onDashRejected` events, and the optional parkour example.
A native ground or mid-air slam as a session grant: define, grant and revoke, the key the player presses, the damage and radius options, impact events and the limits.

pages.title: Overdrive: a Sandevistan-style boost for a shared world
pages.description: Grant a real-time reflex overdrive: the owner moves, swings and reloads faster while nobody else is slowed and no clock is touched. Definitions, tiers, presets, the observer presentation, the rebindable key and the release paths.

Short Circuit, Overheat, Cyberware Malfunction, Cripple Movement, Reboot Optics and Weapon Glitch as kinds of one server-owned upload; Self-ICE, active purge, statuses, protection scopes and the `onHackingTransition` ledger.
Network vehicle identity, streaming, authority leases, seats and proxy replication, doors and glass, damage profiles, and the full asymmetric server and client Lua API.

Mounted weapons in multiplayer: driver authority, shots and damage, supported models, protocol 1.24, current limitations and twelve read-only client Lua APIs for weapon selection, ammo, heat and turret aim.
Exact spawn IDs for 172 vehicle records declaring weapon mounts, with live-tested Basilisk, Outlaw and Shion variants, mount profiles, spawn examples and the machine-readable catalogue.
Server-controlled RGB paint, replication and change events.
Server-owned autonomous driving, optional visible NPC drivers, reserved driver seats, routes, follow and chase, speed, behavior, lifecycle events and simulator handover.
Synchronised session time and weather: the network model, shared configuration, ACL-gated commands, random weather events, and the server and client APIs.
Server-authoritative native lifts: adopting a LiftDevice, bucket and chunk streaming, movement and pause control, late-join catch-up, and the reference resource commands.
Server-owned automatic and interactive doors: dynamic discovery, native animations, elevator landing safety, routing buckets, access rules and client/server Lua exports.
Server-owned world props and lights: creation, streaming and cleanup.

Attach props to player slots or vehicles with local position and rotation. Learn server authority, client rendering, bone discovery, revision-safe handoffs and lifecycle cleanup. Requires matching attachment-capable client/server builds and assets.

pages.title: Props and effects
pages.description: Placing server-owned objects, lights and replicated effects from Lua: the create definition, the curated model catalogue, the bucket and ground-height traps that make a prop invisible, lights and what respawns them, carrying, quotas and removal reasons, with the admin commands and two worked scenes.
Raycasts, ground height, aim rays and nearby object queries.

Use Cyberpunk's native screen fades from client Lua: fade out, hold and return, color options, completion events, resource ownership and automatic recovery. Includes server-coordinated transitions and HUD limitations.

Read the player's vanilla-map waypoint separately from quests and POIs, observe placement and selection events, focus the native map and pick a destination without fast travel. Includes a taxi-sharing example.

pages.title: Drawing in the world
pages.description: Every way a Lua resource puts something at a point in Night City: native ground markers, per-frame world anchors and the native card, ring and dot overlays, the marker-plus-prompt POI facade, proximity zones and nameplates — with lifecycle and cleanup for each.
Vanilla map markers and mappins: creating and updating blips, attaching them to entities, custom icon metadata, stable aliases, and the complete sprite catalogue.
Custom world and NPC prompts: attaching interactions to players or NPCs, multiple actions and hold keys, the definition reference, and keeping server authority intact.
Take the vanilla prompt off a vending machine, ATM, terminal or door panel and put your own shop there: naming a device, ownership, the `open77:deviceUsed` event and every refusal reason.
The open77_worldui facade: a ground marker and its interaction prompt created and destroyed as one owned handle, the definition reference, and the invisible-ring trap it exists to avoid.
The open77_zones service: enter and exit events with hysteresis, the definition reference, the polling model and quotas, and why every containment rule must still be re-derived on the server.
Polygons, boxes, circles and spheres, entity zones and groups: containment queries, entry and exit callbacks, and the in-game zone editor with native debug drawing.
Reusable WebUI toasts: local client notifications, server-targeted delivery, updating and dismissing, queue limits, positions and progress.
Show and hide the game's HUD elements from a client resource.
`open77_uikit`: progress bars, text hints, alerts, input forms, context and keyboard menus and a radial wheel drawn from one page — with the focus rule that outranks the whole feature list.
Register rebindable actions and handle press and hold callbacks.
Take a named input away from the player and give it back — per-action blocks or the whole control stream — with the ownership and release rules that stop a crashed resource stranding somebody.

The bundled ALT context menu: opt-in targeting of players, vehicles, doors, time and weather with resource-registered actions, the weapon-wheel claim it holds, and the exports a gamemode composes it from.

`Open77.camera.screenRay`, `screenRaycast` and `Open77.input.cursor`: resolve the entity under a screen point through the native physics owner, with the identity kinds a client can and cannot promise.

Put the view where your resource wants it: create, place, follow, look at and shake a camera, spectate a player from the server, and the release rules that guarantee the player gets their own view back.
Resource-owned world and entity visual effects plus spatialised sound effects, with inspection, cleanup and the curated alias catalogues.
Play package MP3/WAV assets locally or through server-owned network sounds. Control playback, pause, seek, volume and position with resource-owned handles, routing buckets and late-join timelines.

`open77_sound` plays an audio file your resource ships: spatial behaviour, server twins, ownership and lifetime, why files are never shared across resources, and how it differs from the game's own `Open77.sfx` events.
Chat messages, slash commands, completion, and the built-in developer commands available to every player.
Proximity voice, radio and phone channels, voice-driven lipsync, Lua APIs and settings.
Enable voice-driven mouths on male/female player heads, locally and on replicated players, with resource-owned Lua controls and diagnostics.
The write-only client clipboard API, the clipboard.write permission, failure reasons, and the built-in /pos and /rot transform commands.
Install and declare stack, world and personal mods.

pages.title: Mods your server requires
pages.description: Requiring a mod for your world: whether the content needs a mod at all or is really a Lua resource, the trust verdicts and the capability cap that lets unverified packages carry inert data only, importing from the Warden Mods tab, who hosts the bytes, requesting a review, bandwidth, and removing a mod without stranding players.
Create and preload custom sky hologram advertisements.

pages.title: Writing a gamemode
pages.description: Build an OPEN//77 gamemode with local state-machine files or shared server services, move players safely, isolate rounds in routing buckets, and validate authority and lifecycle.
Modular gamemode architecture: shared server services through asynchronous exports, isolated ownership, generated state-machine patterns and gameplay conventions.
Free-for-all and arena modes, loadouts, bots, scoring and configuration.
Squads, the closing cordon, loot, revives and configuration.

pages.title: Lua API reference
pages.description: Searchable reference for every registered OPEN//77 Lua function, separated by runtime so a client projection is never mistaken for server authority.
NPC templates, vehicle records, seat and door constants, items, weapons, effects, sounds, animations and sprite catalogues, with explicit support levels.

`Open77.data` turns a TweakDB record string into the facts a resource can show — display name, class, manufacturer, seats, quality — the fields each runtime can answer, and the one asymmetry on `npc`.
The ACL-gated in-game Lua laboratory: client execution, native lab commands, the REDscript bridge, and the limits that keep it out of gameplay code.

The MCP server and Claude Code skill that let an AI agent test OPEN//77 in the running game: the tool list, the human-path connection, repeatable scenarios, installation, and the rules that keep a verdict honest.
